summary:
No measure, incident or institution specific to Mardin concerning transgender visitors is documented in this edition's sources. What a trans visitor to Mardin faces is the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in the province is recorded adding bans, checkpoints or enforcement programmes of its own.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts described as contrary to biological sex and general morality carry up to three years imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, with mandatory infertility conditions and evaluation at a government-approved hospital, while imprisoning care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. The package is national in scope and would apply in Mardin as elsewhere.

Drafting activity continued into 2026. A February 2026 press report described legislation under consideration that would criminalise public advocacy of behaviour contrary to biological sex with one to three years imprisonment; that provision was not included in the 12th judicial package. Amnesty International recorded that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible, and that none was ultimately submitted to parliament. The gap between drafting and enactment has not governed enforcement: in 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly twenty trans women in streets, shops and cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for background checks, without fines but with documentation, before release.

The statutory baseline is permissive on its face. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. Marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking placed Türkiye 47th of 49.

Public assembly is a documented risk. Amnesty International recorded that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, that three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and that prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. Pride events have been banned in most years since 2015, with tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions used against those who defied the bans.

Transition-related care is tightening on two fronts. In June 2025 the health ministry's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under twenty-one, despite existing law permitting access from eighteen; a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 additionally barred hospitals from recording the "other" option in medical-board reports and required e-reports, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records.

Organisational space is contracting. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing images deemed obscene and incompatible with society's moral values. In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, nine associations and thirteen businesses.
tangentialFactors:
Türkiye's position has deteriorated against its own recent history rather than against an external benchmark. Decriminalisation dates to 1858 and legal gender recognition to 1988, yet ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking places the country 47th of 49, and the Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions.

The gap between legislative status and street practice is itself a documented pattern. Three draft packages targeting LGBTI people were published in 2025 without being submitted to parliament, and a further advocacy-criminalisation proposal missed the 2026 omnibus, while police checkpoint checks and document demands proceeded throughout.

Official framing supplies the justification. The government's stated position of protecting the family and public morals has been identified by Human Rights Watch as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma, and monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Violence risk remains lethal and asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same national framework with no provincial relief. Marriage eligibility is determined by the gender recorded in the civil registry, so legal gender change alters whom a person may marry; no same-sex marriage or civil union is recognised, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

Access to employment in the armed forces is closed: openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service.

Hormone prescribing for people under twenty-one has been prohibited by the health ministry's medicines agency since June 2025, and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation issued following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular requires e-reports and removes the "other" option from medical-board documentation, restricting and recording transition care.

The 11th Judicial Package, if enacted as leaked, would raise the age floor for gender-affirming care to twenty-five with mandatory infertility conditions and government-approved hospital evaluation, and would penalise both providers and patients.

Organisations face closure: an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association in December 2025, and in September 2026 raids under the 'My Family is Safe' operation produced 162 suspects and targeted nine associations and thirteen businesses. Prosecutions arising from the 2025 pride marches continued against 92 people at year's end.

Prison conditions are governed by registered sex and by isolation rather than gender-matched placement. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; a trans man had been held in a women's prison, and the case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated through Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, reporting delayed medical response, delayed prosecutor and crime-scene access and unrecorded witness statements.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this edition's inventory addresses Mardin province directly: the absence of a local measure here reflects what the audited sources cover, not a verified finding that no local enforcement practice exists.

The status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved in the sources. Human Rights Watch reported it as leaked and pending in October 2025, and the three draft packages of 2025 were not submitted to parliament; whether any provision has since been enacted is not sourced here.

The February 2026 proposal to criminalise public advocacy of behaviour contrary to biological sex is recorded only as under consideration in press reporting, and its subsequent fate is not sourced.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the June 2025 under-twenty-one hormone ban remain in force in their reported form, and whether they restrict care in Mardin specifically, is not documented in these sources.

The outcome of the prosecutions of 92 pride march participants, the appeals status of the İzmir dissolution order, and the findings of any investigation into the Sincan prison death remain unresolved in this inventory.

The Human Rights Watch 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documents beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth; it predates legal changes after 2018 and is not a statement of current law.
